conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to check on how you’re feeling emotionally.  

To do that, I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—better known as the EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that screens for symptoms of depression and anxiety that can show up after having a baby. It also includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.  

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team; the goal is simply to understand what support would help you most. We’ll walk through 10 short questions about the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.  

Ready to begin?  

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Lately… most of the time I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of forced, like I’m going through the motions. I’d say “sometimes,” but definitely not as easily as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I put “sometimes.” I can still laugh, but it feels kind of flat, like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, not very often. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I still try, because I know I “should,” but the spark just isn’t there most days.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more often than I’d like to admit. If the baby’s fussy or won’t nap, I automatically think it’s something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not soothing him right. Even little stuff, like dropping a burp cloth, turns into me telling myself I’m a lousy mom. I’d say it happens “yes, quite often.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything’s quiet, my mind keeps circling—Is he breathing? Am I doing this right? What if I miss something? I know the thoughts aren’t logical, but I can’t shut them off. I’d check “yes, very often.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—my heart races, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even when everything looks fine. It’s happened maybe two or three times this week. I’d say “yes, sometimes.”
Things have been getting on top of me
Yes—most days. Between feedings, laundry, trying to sleep, and still feeling like I’m falling behind, it all piles up. I manage to keep the basics done, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
Yes, several nights this week. I lie there feeling heavy and sad, replaying everything I think I did wrong, and it takes me forever to nod off. Then when the baby wakes, it’s hard to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… most of the time. I wake up already feeling like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. It’s not every single minute, but it’s definitely more good moments than bad right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after a middle-of-the-night feeding when I couldn’t get back to sleep and just felt overwhelmed. Another time my partner asked how I was doing and the tears started before I could answer.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes… it has flickered through my mind once or twice—like a quick “what if I weren’t here” thought—but I push it away. I don’t have any plan or real wish to act on it; it’s more this fleeting, scary idea that pops up when everything feels too heavy.

You've shared that over the past week laughter feels flat, activities you once enjoyed now seem like chores, and a persistent "gray cloud" of sadness and self-blame hangs over you, interrupted only by near-constant worry and occasional panic. You're working hard to care for your baby, yet you feel overwhelmed, cry easily, sleep poorly, and have fleeting scary thoughts of not being here, all while still managing to push through each day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter feels "flat" and requires conscious effort, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>She explicitly reports "the spark just isn't there most days" and only rare enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "quite often" for everyday mishaps, aligning with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive worries that persist even when circumstances are calm, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "barely treading water," aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty on multiple nights this week due to persistent sadness and rumination, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the time" and describes a persistent gloomy mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 21 (≥14) plus a score ≥1 on Item 10 signals high risk for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You describe <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the time, <sym>self-reproach</sym>, near-constant <sym>anxiety</sym> with panic symptoms, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> linked to mood, meeting DSM-5 criteria threshold for further evaluation. Passive suicidal ideation warrants immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>OB</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you tonight for support until professional help is secured
4. Begin basic self-care: eat small frequent meals, hydrate, and rest when baby sleeps; limit stimulating screens before bed
5. Consider 5-minute paced breathing or gentle stretching when <sym>panic sensations</med> rise; practice when not distressed to build familiarity
6. Explore local postpartum support groups (e.g., Postpartum Support International warmline 1-800-944-4PPD) for peer encouragement
7. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks with your provider to monitor symptom trend after intervention starts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 4–6 wks post-delivery; bottle- or breast-feeding (not specified).

Responses to EPDS-10:

Affect/Enjoyment  
• Reduced ability to laugh or look forward to activities; describes “flat” pleasure.

Mood  
• Persistent sadness or “gray cloud”; frequent crying episodes (≥2 this week).

Cognitive Themes  
• Marked self-blame/feelings of inadequacy as a mother (“lousy mom”).

Anxiety  
• Near-constant intrusive worry; multiple un-cued panic symptoms (HR, tremor); occurring “very often.”

Sleep  
• Mood-related initial and middle insomnia; difficulty re-settling after infant wakes.

Coping  
• Feels “on top of me most days”; sense of treading water.

Safety  
• Fleeting passive self-harm thoughts (“what if I weren’t here”) without intent or plan; no reported protective factors explored.

Pattern Summary  
Consistent symptoms of low mood, anhedonia, pathologic guilt, prominent anxiety/panic, and functional overwhelm beginning post-delivery. Passive suicidal ideation present.

Screening Impression  
High clinical concern for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment warranted. Recommend expedited referral to OB mental-health team or psychiatry for comprehensive evaluation and formulation.

Safety Plan Reviewed: ☐ Yes ☐ No (to be completed by evaluating clinician)
